title: Sasai: He made the world
hook: a chair on a carpenter's bench: the Patti's first letter says the world was made, and its Maker is the one Master of all

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Patti, the tablet: Guru Nanak's poem with a line of wisdom for each letter. Your line was letter by letter. What big thing did you start with one small piece? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five.

Sawdust on the floor, a half-built chair on the bench, and a carpenter running a thumb along a joint to feel whether it sits true. Nobody in that workshop would say the chair happened. It's being made: measured, cut, fitted, on purpose. The Patti, the alphabet poem we opened yesterday, starts with a maker's word like that, and uses it for the whole world. Its first letter is sasai, the letter S. Today: Sasai, and the hand that made things.
screen: `A THUMBPRINT IN THE GLAZE.` → `SOMEBODY'S HAND WAS HERE.` → `THE PATTI'S FIRST LETTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the first stanza, in paraphrase: S. The One who fashioned the world is the one Master of all. Those whose minds stay fixed in that One's service, their coming into the world bears fruit. First, the word for made. The line says saajee, fashioned, shaped, put together. It's a maker's word, the way a carpenter or a potter makes. The world, in this first letter, isn't an accident lying around. It has been put together on purpose. Second, one Master of all. Sabhnaa, of all of them. Not a master for the rich and another for the poor. Not one for this village and another for the next. Some readers draw a quiet claim from that: if the same hand made everyone, nobody belongs to a different owner. And it sits on the first line of an alphabet. Third, look what the stanza does next. It doesn't stop at admiring creation. It turns to the person reading. Those who serve with their minds attached, their coming is fruitful. Safal, bearing fruit. The question shifts from who made the world to what you'll do in it. Fourth, why start here. A school slate could begin with anything. Guru Nanak's begins with the Maker, before anything else is learned. Every letter after this one is read in that light. It's worth noticing on a busy weekday: the coffee cup, the sidewalk, the person in line ahead of you, all fall under the same first letter. Today's line: he made it.
screen: `SAAJEE: FASHIONED, LIKE A POTTER'S WORK.` · `ONE MASTER OF ALL.` · `SERVICE MAKES A LIFE BEAR FRUIT.` · `EVERY LETTER READ IN THIS LIGHT.` · then, large: `HE MADE IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the world as made. Let your eyes rest on whatever is near you: a plant, your own hand, a window, the sky through it. Choose one thing and look at it as if it had been shaped on purpose. Notice its edges, its color, how it holds together. Then look at the next thing the same way. No need to explain anything. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, wonderful Lord, as you look. If you don't, just let each thing be something someone could have made with care. The bell holds the time.
Sasai. The letter S, the Patti's first letter: the One who fashioned the world is the one Master of all, and serving that One makes a life bear fruit. Today's word.

Your line: he made it. This week we read with a pandit, stood by a river, learned that deeds are written, closed the Oankar and opened the Patti. Today, treat one ordinary thing as made, and one person as made by the same hand as you. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of God as Karta Purakh, the Creator, and the Patti, sung in Raga Asa, opens with that thought on its first letter; the idea that one Creator made everyone is taught as a basis for equality and seva.

original.note: sasai: by the letter S; the word that opens the first stanza of Guru Nanak's Patti.

trapdoor: what you thought: sasai is just the name of a letter.

what a scholar hears: saajee is a maker's verb, and sabhnaa, of all, makes the Master everyone's; the stanza ends on service, safal, bearing fruit.
